statement: Positive numbers $a$ and $b$ with $a > b$ satisfy $a^2 + b^2 = 6ab$. What is the value of $\dfrac{a + b}{a - b}$?

choices.misconception: I forgot the $2ab$ when expanding $(a + b)^2$, so I got $6ab$ over $4ab$ under the square root.
I found that the square of the fraction is $8ab \div 4ab = 2$ and forgot to take the square root.
I worked out $(a + b)^2 = 8ab$, took the square root of 8 and never dealt with $a - b$.
I solved for the ratio $a \div b$ and gave that instead of the fraction asked for.

hints: Look at the square of the fraction instead of the fraction.
Solving for $a \div b$ works but gives nested roots. Instead, write $(a + b)^2$ and $(a - b)^2$ using the given equation, so both become multiples of $ab$.

solutions.reliable: From the equation, $(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = 6ab + 2ab = 8ab$ and $(a - b)^2 = 6ab - 2ab = 4ab$. So the square of the fraction is $8ab \div 4ab = 2$. Because $a > b > 0$, the fraction is positive, so it equals $\sqrt{2}$. Check by solving: dividing the equation by $b^2$ gives $t^2 - 6t + 1 = 0$ for $t = a \div b$, so $t = 3 + 2\sqrt{2}$, and $(t + 1) \div (t - 1) = (4 + 2\sqrt{2}) \div (2 + 2\sqrt{2}) = \sqrt{2}$. The transferable idea: when a condition is symmetric, square the target so both parts can be written with the same building blocks.

whyOnTest: Squaring the target turns an awkward ratio into two short expansions, while the direct route through $a \div b$ needs careful root arithmetic.
